clue.text: Fiery character with degree retained as old guide

indicators.note: retained says the degree is held inside the fiery character

parts.note: a dragon breathes fire, so it is a fiery character
MA is a Master of Arts degree

explanation.surface: A hot-headed person with a university qualification is cast as a guide from the past.
explanation.definitionFit: A dragoman was an interpreter and guide in Middle Eastern countries, mostly in Ottoman times.

clue.text: Unchaste woman's under control outside

indicators.note: outside puts the words for under control around the woman

parts.note: led means guided, kept under control
W is the abbreviation for woman; the 's stands for is

explanation.surface: A woman described as kept in check yet morally loose, a moralising picture of control.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewd describes lustful, sexually immodest behaviour, the opposite of chaste.

clue.text: Feels a little pretentious what the judges are wearing

indicators.note: a little of the word pretentious is just its opening letter

parts.note: judges wear robes in court

explanation.surface: Someone senses a touch of pomposity in the judges' courtroom attire.
explanation.definitionFit: To probe is to feel around exploratively, as a doctor probes a wound.

clue.text: Trouble from a number of spectators (it's been contained)

indicators.note: been contained says it is held within the crowd figure

parts.note: the gate is the number of people attending a sports match
it, with the 's standing for has

explanation.surface: A disturbance arising from the crowd, with an aside that it was kept under control.
explanation.definitionFit: To agitate is to disturb or stir up, the verb sense of trouble.

clue.text: Money behind you, not outside (though you can't count it).

parts.note: M is an abbreviation for money, as in economists' M0 and M3
a behind is the backside, an ass

indicators.note: outside puts the word for not around the letter for you

parts.note: non is Latin for not, familiar from words like nonsense
U sounds like you, as in text speak

explanation.surface: Cash at your back that isn't on the outside, with a parenthetic shrug that it can't be counted.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a grammar joke: a mass noun, like rice or advice, is one that is uncountable.
explanation.definitionFit: In grammar a mass noun is uncountable, taking no plural, unlike a count noun.

clue.text: Old Bill turned up at empty school! It hurts to show efficiency?

indicators.note: in a down clue turned up means read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: neb is a bird's bill or beak

indicators.note: an empty school keeps only its outside letters

parts.note: ouch is what you say when it hurts

explanation.surface: The police arrive at a deserted school, then a cry of pain and a wry question about efficiency.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Bill is British slang for the police, but here it splits into O and a bird's bill. 'turned up' makes BENO.
explanation.definitionFit: To be no slouch is an idiom for being quick and capable at something.

clue.text: When upset, flake out

parts.note: as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: to flake is to peel off in layers

explanation.surface: Someone told to collapse in exhaustion when they're distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flake out' reads as one phrase meaning collapse, but splits: flake is wordplay, out the definition. 'upset' gives LEEP.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone out cold or out for the count is asleep or unconscious.

clue.text: Carelessly forget covering note — he's for the high jump!

indicators.note: covering says the anagram goes around the note
carelessly says the letters of forget are thrown together anyhow

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A careless slip over a memo means someone faces punishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for the high jump' is British slang for about to be punished; here it is literal, as the creature leaps high. 'Carelessly' gives TEFROG, which goes around RE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tree frogs are agile climbing frogs that leap between branches, a literal high jumper.

clue.text: Hesitates to dismiss original claims

indicators.note: dismissing the original means dropping the first letter

parts.note: to waver is to hesitate

explanation.surface: Someone dithers about throwing out first versions of their assertions.
explanation.definitionFit: To aver is to state firmly or assert, so avers is a synonym of claims.

clue.text: Old Charlie's left behind bars

indicators.note: left here is the past of leave, saying the letter departs

parts.note: caged means locked up behind bars
Charlie is C in the NATO phonetic alphabet; the 's stands for has

explanation.surface: An elderly man called Charlie has been left in prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Aged is a straightforward synonym for old or elderly.

clue.text: Stay here and be late, most unexpectedly

indicators.note: unexpectedly signals the letters turn up in a surprising new order

explanation.surface: An invitation to linger, arriving late and very unexpectedly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unexpectedly' rearranges BE LATE MOST. The Bates Motel is where the guests meet their end in Hitchcock's Psycho, so the cheerful invitation is darkly ironic.
explanation.definitionFit: A motel is a place to stay overnight; this one is the notorious lodging in the film Psycho.

clue.text: Writing about previous measures seems suspicious

indicators.note: about here means turned round, so the abbreviation is read backwards

parts.note: MS is short for manuscript, a piece of writing
the ell was an old unit of length for cloth

explanation.surface: A document concerning outdated measurements arouses doubt.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that smells, as in 'it smells fishy', gives an impression of being dodgy.

clue.text: Race boldly run that's closely contested

indicators.note: run here means handled or arranged, so the letters are set out anew

explanation.surface: A race run with daring that ends up a tight contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'closely' means between near neighbours, not narrowly; 'Race' looks like the definition but is fodder. In Britain a local derby is a match between two clubs from the same area.
explanation.definitionFit: A local derby is a match between neighbouring teams, so geographically close rivals contest it.

clue.text: Throw in drink for writer

indicators.note: in says the throw is placed inside the drink

parts.note: to tope is to drink heavily
to roll dice is to throw them

explanation.surface: Someone tosses a drink in, cheers to an author.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope was a prolific Victorian novelist, author of the Barchester novels.

clue.text: Put on a decent spread

indicators.note: spread says the letters are laid out in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone lays out a respectable buffet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' looks like a meal set out on a table, but it shuffles A DECENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A play is put on or enacted when it is staged and performed.

clue.text: Agent's failure during dodgy year

indicators.note: during places the failure within the jumbled year
dodgy means unreliable, so the letters are suspect and rearranged

parts.note: a miss is a failure to hit

explanation.surface: A secret agent's blunder in a bad year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Agent's failure' reads as one phrase, but the 's is 'is', splitting the definition off. 'dodgy' makes EARY.
explanation.definitionFit: An emissary is a person sent on a mission as a representative or agent.

clue.text: Instinctively recognises northern types round town

indicators.note: round says the northern peoples go around the town's letter

parts.note: the Inuit are peoples of the Arctic north
T is the abbreviation for town

explanation.surface: Someone senses by gut feel which Arctic peoples are near a settlement.
explanation.definitionFit: To intuit is to know or perceive something by instinct rather than reasoning.

clue.text: Fuss about arresting that man — him?

indicators.note: arresting means catching and holding, so the man is put inside

parts.note: a to-do is a fuss
he is the pronoun for that man
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A commotion over a man being arrested, ending with a pointed question about who.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition 'him?' is an example of a male name, flagged by the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Theodore is a man's name, so it is one possible identity for the 'him' referred to.

clue.text: Home failing to accommodate Oscar or Bill

parts.note: in means at home

indicators.note: to accommodate means to make room for, so the letter goes inside

parts.note: a vice is a failing or moral weakness
Oscar is O in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A household unable to put up an award or a man named Bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oscar or Bill' reads like two people's names; Bill is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An invoice is a bill requesting payment for goods or services.

clue.text: Is no trouble suppressing demand for vegetable

indicators.note: suppressing means holding down or containing, so the demand sits inside
trouble means disturb, so the letters are stirred up

parts.note: a call is a demand, as in a call for action

explanation.surface: It's easy to hold back demand for a vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is no trouble' reads as 'easy', but 'trouble' is the anagram signal making SION.
explanation.definitionFit: A scallion is a spring onion, a green vegetable.

clue.text: Caught on record in middle of America

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
to enter is to record, as in entering data

explanation.surface: Something is caught on tape somewhere in the heart of the US.
explanation.definitionFit: Center is the American spelling of centre, the middle; 'of America' flags the US form.

clue.text: Bloke Hearts picked up — their number 4 — is top scorer

indicators.note: picked up means took on board, so the male holds the card suit

parts.note: a bloke is a male
H is the abbreviation for hearts in card games
their refers to Hearts, and the fourth letter of that word is R

explanation.surface: A man signed by Hearts, the Edinburgh football club, wears their number 4 shirt and leads the scoring.
explanation.walkthrough: Hearts is a Scottish football club, and 'top scorer' sounds like a striker; here it is a composer who writes scores.
explanation.definitionFit: Gustav Mahler was a leading composer, and a composer writes musical scores.

clue.text: Female reveller, one in West End dropping a tab

parts.note: Mae West was the Hollywood actress

indicators.note: dropping is drug slang for swallowing, here meaning the letter is removed
in says one goes inside the word end

parts.note: taken as written
A means one, as in a single item
a tab is a tablet, and E is slang for an ecstasy tablet

explanation.surface: A clubber in London's West End popping a pill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End' is not London's theatre district: West leads to Mae West. 'in' gives ENAD, and 'dropping' removes the E (an ecstasy tablet), leaving NAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A maenad was a frenzied female follower of Dionysus, god of wine and revelry.

clue.text: 19, say, is low mark

parts.note: under means below, low down
19 is INVOICE, a bill, and score is an old word for a bill or reckoning

explanation.surface: A bill is described as a poor grade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'low mark' reads as a poor grade; low is wordplay and mark the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An underscore is a line drawn beneath text, a typographical mark.

clue.text: Activity on board — can money talk?

indicators.note: talk asks for the words to be heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: can is slang for toilet, a loo, and dough is slang for money

explanation.surface: A question of whether cash can speak during a board game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'money talk' suggests money talks; instead loo plus dough, said out loud, gives the game.
explanation.definitionFit: Ludo is a children's board game played with dice and counters.

clue.text: Go climbing in one film

indicators.note: climbing says the hidden letters are read backwards
in says the answer is found inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: An invitation to head up a mountain in a single movie.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft left 'in' as a link word, but it is the hiding signal: the letters sit in 'one film', and 'climbing' reads them upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Go means energy or vigour, as in 'full of go', which is the same as full of life.

clue.text: Glower from revolutionary about to receive award

indicators.note: to receive means to take in, so the award goes inside
revolutionary means turning round, so the word is reversed

parts.note: re means about or concerning
the MBE is a British honour, Member of the Order of the British Empire

explanation.surface: A rebel scowls about being given an honour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Glower' looks like scowl but means something that glows.
explanation.definitionFit: An ember is a smouldering coal that still glows, so it is literally a glower.

clue.text: Conservative sought election as democrat — that's novel

parts.note: to run for office is to seek election
for can mean as, as in 'took him for a fool'

explanation.surface: A Tory stood for office as a Democrat, which is something new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like an adjective, new; it is the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Cranford is an 1853 novel by Elizabeth Gaskell about a small English town.
